faqs.q: Coyotes are in our St. Petersburg neighborhood — will trapping help?
faqs.a: Rarely, and we will explain why rather than sell it. Urban coyote territories refill — remove one pair and the next disperses into the vacancy within weeks, while the attractants (outdoor pet food, unsecured trash, free-roaming cats) keep teaching them the route. What works is the city's playbook: cats indoors, dogs leashed, food secured, and confident hazing of bold animals. A coyote that is sick, injured, or genuinely dangerous is a call to the city and FWC. Our work is the raccoon in your attic; the coyote file belongs to coexistence, and honestly run, it works.

faqs.q: Bats are in our downtown Clearwater building — how does a commercial exclusion work?
faqs.a: Survey first, at dusk, to count exits and identify the colony — Brazilian free-tailed bats are the downtown default across Tampa Bay. Then, inside the legal window of August 15 to April 15, one-way devices go on the active exits, the building is confirmed empty over several nights, all openings are sealed, and guano is cleaned with proper precautions. Outside the window we survey and prep so the legal-season job is short. For a commercial building, the documentation — counts, photos, sealed-entry map — is part of the deliverable your facilities file needs.

faqs.q: What should I do about armadillo digging in Largo?
faqs.a: Nine-banded armadillos dig for grubs and earthworms in lawns and flower beds, and they are common throughout most of Florida, including Largo. A live-trapped armadillo may be released on-site, or released within the same county on 40 or more contiguous acres with the landowner's written permission, within 24 hours — those are the Florida rules, and we follow them. We also talk through fencing and grub management, because trapping alone rarely ends digging in good habitat.

faqs.q: Rats are in our Pinellas Park horse barn — same as a house job?
faqs.a: Same principles, farm application. Feed goes into metal cans, the barn's eave and door gaps get hardware cloth, and we trap the resident rats with nonchemical methods while the food discipline takes hold — a barn feeding twenty rats a night cannot be trapped clean until the buffet closes. Because barns stay semi-open by design, the goal is a rat-hostile barn: sealed feed, no harborage piles, traps at the runs. We quote it as a barn program, separate from any house sealing, after walking both.

faqs.q: I found a big snake in my Dunedin yard — what kind is it likely to be?
faqs.a: Most Florida snakes are nonvenomous and beneficial, and identification comes first. The venomous snakes in most of Florida are the cottonmouth, eastern diamondback rattlesnake, dusky pygmy rattlesnake, and harlequin coralsnake. A large, docile black snake may be an eastern indigo snake, which is federally Threatened — leave it alone, photograph it from a distance, and call FWC. Never handle a snake you cannot identify, and call us for an identification before anyone tries to move it.

faqs.q: Raccoons own our Tarpon Springs dock area — what changes that?
faqs.a: The waste stream. Dock raccoons are professionals sustained by fish scraps, sponge-dock dumpsters, and pet food on porches; trapping thins them for a week. Locking dumpster lids, hosing cleaning stations into contained drains, and feeding no animal outdoors rewrites the dock's economics, and then trapping removes the residents who remain. We build both halves — the discipline changes with the business or homeowner, the trapping and dock-den exclusion with us — and the bayou goes back to herons.

faqs.q: Why is Safety Harbor squirrel work different from other towns?
faqs.a: The canopy never breaks. Philippe Park's oaks connect to the neighborhood oaks, which connect to your roof — a gray squirrel can commute the whole town at canopy height, so individual trapping without complete, metal-backed sealing simply rotates the population through your attic. Safety Harbor jobs are therefore seal-first in philosophy: trap the current tenants, close every corner and vent with materials that survive chewing, and trim the bridges. In this canopy, the seal is the service; the trap is the footnote.
